title: Laziness in disguise
hookLine: busyness with pointless things is also laziness (Bodhicaryavatara 7)
tomorrow: so where does the strength come from?

cards: By ten at night the to-do app looks great. Inbox cleared. Desktop tidied.
Three videos on how to be more productive, watched all the way through. Every box ticked except the one that mattered. Somewhere under all that tidying, a single page sat open, unfinished.
It felt busy all evening. It felt like work. So was it effort?
Shantideva has a sharp opinion, and an older Buddhist story offers another voice worth hearing.

teach.b: Shantideva names laziness in three forms: plain idleness, clinging to worthless things, and despondency, the voice that says I can't. The middle one is the disguise.

You can be very busy with things that lead nowhere and still be lazy, in his sense, because the good thing is still waiting. He presses with urgency: time is short, so why spend it on what doesn't matter?
Its best case is strong. Busyness can be the most respectable way to avoid what scares us. Now the other voice, from the Pali texts.
A monk named Sona pushed so hard in practice that he wanted to quit. The Buddha asked him: you used to play the lute. When the strings were too tight, did it sound good?
Tuned just right? Yes. Effort, he said, is like that.
Its best case is strong too: strain isn't virtue, and a string wound too tight snaps. Side by side, they aren't fighting. Shantideva warns against slack strings dressed up as busy hands.
The lute warns against strings wound so tight they break.

teach.h: DID THE GOOD THING GET MY ENERGY?
teach.b: Both ask an evening the same question: did the good thing get my energy, or only the look of it?

how: Buddhist teachers often pair Shantideva's warning about laziness with the Buddha's lute advice to Sona, presenting right effort as balanced: neither slack nor strained.

o: pretending to be sick so you can skip work
keeping busy with useless things while the good waits
resting when you're tired instead of pushing on

games.q: laziness and the lute — tap the pairs.
p: the voice that says i can't
not too tight, not too loose

s: for Shantideva, being very busy proves you're not lazy
clinging to worthless things is one of his three forms of laziness.
in the Pali story, the Buddha compares effort to lute strings tuned just right
too tight or too loose, the lute sounds wrong; effort is the same.

games.q: your friend says: 'Shantideva's too harsh. the Buddha told Sona not to overtighten, so the couch is fine.' what's the best case for her side?
o: strain isn't virtue: a string wound too tight snaps, so balance belongs to real effort.
the Buddha taught that effort doesn't matter as long as you feel calm.
busy little tasks are restful, so they're exactly the balance Sona needed.
games.why: the lute story's strength is balance. Shantideva would agree strain isn't the goal; his warning is about busyness pretending to be the good work.

practice: Name one thing you've been busy with that leads nowhere: a scroll, a re-sort, a tab you keep refreshing. Then name the good thing it's crowding out, and one small first step toward it for tomorrow.
Hold the three in mind together, the empty task, the good task, the first step, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Laziness in disguise: in Shantideva's list, clinging to worthless things while the good thing waits. Busy hands, slack strings.

orig.note: Sanskrit: laziness, idleness; Shantideva's word for effort's opposite.

carryVoice: Here's the line: busy isn't effort; the good thing gets the energy. Two days into chapter seven.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 7.2-7.4 (three forms of laziness; attachment to worthless things; urgency)
Vinaya, Mahavagga 5.1; Anguttara Nikaya 6.55 (Sona and the lute)
